newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist-Communist ties cool as polls rise.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist-Communist ties cool as polls rise.

text.p: Ties between France's Socialist and Communist parties cooled on Friday as they jostled over policy after opinion polls showed a real chance of an upset left-wing win in the May 21-June 1 parliamentary election.

The Socialists, by far the strongest partner in the left-wing coalition, have increasingly indicated they would push through their own election platform and ignore the Communists' more radical agenda in case of victory.

Some media said Socialist leader Lionel Jospin had already decided not to include Communist chief Robert Hue in a left-wing cabinet even though the Communists would have contributed to an election win.
The spat came out into the open with the Communists criticising Jospin for seeking to impose "hegemony" on the left and the party's newspaper refusing to publish an open letter by Jospin to voters.
The snub was the latest sign of tension between the two left-wing opposition allies in the run-up to the snap parliamentary election called by President Jacques Chirac.
The daily L'Humanite, which failed to publish Jospin's article, had earlier published the full text of an article by Chirac attacking the left's record and programme on Wednesday.
"This sort of exchange of letters turns the election into a sort of presidentialisation which is inappropriate," the outgoing Communist National Assembly floor leader Alain Bocquet said.
"It is desirable that the left which wins the parliamentary elections should be a balanced left. For the left to succeed, we need a more influential Communist party," he told RTL radio.

The Communists, who oppose a single European currency, were angered when Jospin pledged this week that if the left won the Socialists would impose their broadly favourable line on European economic and monetary union on left-wing partners.
Communist leader Robert Hue has hinted that his party might make a referendum on the single currency a condition for supporting a Socialist-led government.
"Is victory possible? I believe it is, but nothing is decided," the 59-year-old Jospin told RMC radio.
"The trend is in our favour, we are on an upwards trend," he said after a poll on Thursday showed the ruling centre-right's campaign lead had almost vanished in the National Assembly.
The Ipsos poll showed the ruling centre-right with 290 of the 577 seats, the Socialists 264, the Communists 22 and the National Front one.
It was the narrowest lead for Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition since Chirac, elected to a seven-year term ending in 2002, gambled his presidency by calling the early election.
Juppe said on Friday he wanted a change of tone from personal barbs and would focus his campaign more on jobs.

"What I deeply desire is for the campaign to change tone," he told France 3 television. "Over the past two weeks it has largely consisted of personal attacks and partisan jibes. The time for such behaviour is over," he said.
"Unemployment should be at the heart of the campaign," he added. Unemployment in France is running at 12.8 percent, a post-war record.
Juppe, deeply unpopular among voters, has come under fire even from political allies over a lacklustre campaign.
Voters, weary of political sleaze and rising unemployment, dumped the Socialists in the last National Assembly elections in 1993. Both factors now threaten Juppe's coalition.
